newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Papua New Guinea's deputy PM Haiveta retains seat.
newsitem.headline: Papua New Guinea's deputy PM Haiveta retains seat.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's Deputy Prime Minister Chris Haiveta has bucked an anti-incumbent trend in the South Pacific nation's general election to retain his seat in parliament.

Haiveta survived the odium of a mercenary scandal that saw Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan, Defence Minister Mathias Ijape and acting prime minister John Giheno -- who was also mines minister -- lose their seats.

Haiveta, who also holds the post of finance minister, was declared the winner in his south coast Gulf Regional seat late on Saturday with a margin of more than 3,000 seats over his nearest rival. He immediately offered himself as a candidate for prime minister.
"I am ready to take the top post and we are now consolidating our numbers," he said in a statement.
Two weeks of voting in the general election closed on June 28 but because of Papua New Guinea's rugged mountain terrain final results will not be officially declared until July 15.
Haiveta said his party, Pangu, was likely to remain in a coalition with Chan's People's Progress Party (PPP) to try to form the next government.

Political analysts say the likely opposition to Haiveta's claim for the top job will come from Papua New Guinea's first prime minister, Sir Michael Somare, whose National Alliance is likely to tie up with other opposition parties.

Chan and other ministers lost their seats in the 109-seat parliament in a wave of discontent over Chan's US$36 million plan to use African mercenaries to end the secessionist rebellion on the copper-rich island of Bougainville.
Disclosure of the mercenary deal in March sparked an army mutiny and street riots and Chan stood down as prime minister in favour of Giheno while an official inquiry was held.
He reclaimed the prime ministership in early June, saying the inquiry had cleared him.

Papua New Guinea's splintered party system and the fact that less than one-third of the 2,370 candidates ran on party tickets means the new government will not be automatically formed, but will emerge only after political haggling by successful candidates.
The prime ministership will also be decided through political haggling by parliamentarians.
